claims.claim: 20 t-tests on noise, 2,000 repetitions: at least one p < 0.05 in 66% of repetitions.
claims.source: Simulated with NumPy 2.4.6 and SciPy 1.17.1 in this repository.

concept_html:
At a 5% significance level, each test of a true null hypothesis has a 5% chance of a false positive. Run 20 such tests and the chance of at least one false positive is 1 - 0.95**20 = 0.64. A simulation in this course's build agreed: 20 t-tests on pure noise, repeated 2,000 times, gave at least one "significant" result 66% of the time.

Survey reports run many tests by default: every brand, every region, every age band, every wave. Some cells will light up by chance every time.

Adjust the p-values for the number of tests in the family. In statsmodels 0.14:

from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
reject, p_adj, _, _ = multipletests(p_values, alpha=0.05, method="holm")
  • Bonferroni multiplies each p-value by the number of tests m. Simple and strict.
  • Holm is a step-down version of Bonferroni. It controls the same error (any false positive in the family) and always rejects at least as many hypotheses. Prefer it to Bonferroni.
  • Benjamini-Hochberg (method="fdr_bh") controls the false discovery rate: the expected share of false positives among the results you flag. It is less strict and suits screening many cells for follow-up.

For p-values 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.04 and 0.20, Bonferroni and Holm reject only the first. Benjamini-Hochberg rejects the first four.

Define the family before you look: "the 12 regional comparisons in this chart". Adjust within it. Choosing the family after seeing the results defeats the point.

Two habits that reduce the problem at the source:

  • Pre-register the few comparisons that answer the business question. Test those. Label the rest as exploratory.
  • Report how many tests you ran. "3 of 40 regions changed significantly" reads very differently from "Region 7 changed significantly".

lines: def flag_regions(p_values: dict[str, float], alpha: float = 0.05) -> dict[str, float]:
"""Holm-adjusted p-values for one family of regional tests, flagged below alpha."""
regions = list(p_values)
reject, p_adj, _, _ = multipletests([p_values[r] for r in regions], alpha=alpha, method="holm")
return {r: float(p) for r, p, rej in zip(regions, p_adj, reject, strict=True) if rej}

Write `holm_adjust(p_values: list[float]) -> list[float]` without statsmodels. Return adjusted p-values **in the input order**.

1. Sort the p-values ascending. For the k-th smallest (k from 0), compute `min(1, (m - k) * p)`, where `m` is the number of p-values.

exercises.solution:
def holm_adjust(p_values: list[float]) -> list[float]:
    """Holm step-down adjusted p-values, in input order.

    Args:
        p_values: Raw p-values for one family of tests.

    Returns:
        Adjusted p-values, same order as the input.
    """
    m = len(p_values)
    order = sorted(range(m), key=lambda i: p_values[i])
    adjusted = [0.0] * m
    running = 0.0
    for k, i in enumerate(order):
        running = max(running, min(1.0, (m - k) * p_values[i]))
        adjusted[i] = running
    return adjusted

title: Many tests, and the false positives they bring
why_html:
A monthly tracker tested 14 brands in 9 regions, 126 tests, each at 5%. Every month about six cells were flagged in red on the dashboard. Regional managers were asked to explain their red cells. The following month, different cells turned red. Nobody could explain the pattern, because there was none: 126 tests at 5% produce about six false positives by chance.

Holm adjustment within each brand's family of 9 regions removed nearly all the monthly red cells. The few that remained repeated in the next month.
